title: The husband who walked out in 1829
text: Ten years after Ludovicus Szathmáry left his wife Catharina Tóth and their four children, the church was still circulating his description across two dioceses: short, lean, pale, black-haired, a bad left eye, three languages besides his own. His wife's theory was that he got tired of home life and went back to the religion and the county he came from.

title: A seminarian goes missing
text: Franciscus Pap Vásárhelyi left the seminary on 21 May 1839 and did not come back. The vicar general asked every parish priest in the diocese to keep an eye out.

title: Priests skipping the district meeting
text: The May 1839 meeting at N. Kapos was so thinly attended that the vicar general demanded written excuses from every absentee.

title: Homework on kinship
text: The canon-law thesis for 1839 made every priest in the diocese explain stem, degree and line of consanguinity in writing. It is the same arithmetic this rebuild runs on.

title: A price list for sacraments
text: Parishioners complained about fees often enough that in February 1838 the bishop fixed one tariff for the whole diocese, from banns to funeral sermons, with weddings and burials priced by social standing.

title: The red silk veil
text: Between two diocesan circulars someone recorded a local event: on 25 August 1838 Miss Theresia Kulin gave the church a red silk veil worked with flowers. It is the only entry in the ten pages that was written about the parish itself.

title: Reading list by decree
text: The bishop doubled as a subscription agent: a Kassa bookseller's Hungarian edition of a French polemic on the Church of England, a Czech theological journal from Prague, a Pécs bishop's sermons. Each district was expected to buy at least one copy.

title: An underage wedding reaches Buda
text: A schoolmaster's son was married too young, the case went up to the Lieutenancy Council, and every parish got a reminder about the lawful age for marriage. Names in this entry are read with low confidence.

title: A Slovak form filled in Hungarian
text: The Belža entries survive as a later hand copy on a pre-printed Slovak form. The copyist ignored the printed headings, wrote Hungarian ones above them, and put legitimacy in the religion column and sex in the column meant for place of birth.

title: A village of boats and geese
text: From the Senné municipal history (lead L-012): when the rivers flooded, villagers dammed the hollows and took the fish as the water fell, and hunted deer and hares stranded on hummocks from dugout boats. Every family is said to have owned a boat into the interwar years, and the village goose flock ran to nearly six thousand birds until 1975.

title: A fisherman from Lake Constance
text: The same history says a Swiss fisherman was brought to Senné in the 1930s by the Sztáray family and introduced long seine nets to the marsh.

title: Twins, two crosses, and the name used again
text: György Demkó and Mária Hreskó had twin boys in May 1873, Mihály and János. Both names carry a cross in the register. The couple named a son János in 1875 and a son Mihály in 1882.

title: Two pages too early
text: Above the 1873 baptism of Mihály Hornyák the clerk admits the entry was written two pages ahead of where it belonged.

title: One register, three scripts
text: The same parish book is kept in Latin in 1831, Hungarian from 1834, and Cyrillic in 1857, when the priest of Lekárt entered a Viszoka baptism. The death note beside it, six weeks later, is back in Latin letters.

title: Baptised by the other rite, with permission
text: In 1831 Georgius Demko, son of a Greek Catholic father, was baptised by the Latin-rite parish priest of Pálóc, who noted that he had the consent of the local parish priest.

title: A seventeen-year-old gets his papers
text: The certificate that proves Štefan Duska's parents was issued at Senné on 19 August 1947, with a revenue stamp and the parish seal, when he was seventeen. Three years later his mother was buried in Montréal.

title: Alona, who was Anna
text: The owner filed the 1816 Krak baptism under the name Alona. The child in the entry is Anna.

title: András twice
text: János Kóreny and Mária Krak of Jesztreb baptised a son András in 1844 and another, entered in Cyrillic as Andrej, in 1852.

title: A date that corrects its own label
text: A file labelled "maybe 1876" carries a note that the child died on 27 February 1870, two days after the baptism.

title: The page header at last
text: After thirty-odd strips cut from the middle of pages, one includes the printed Hungarian headings of the register: running number, month and day of birth and of baptism, name, sex, legitimacy, parents' names with religion and standing, residence and house number, godparents, baptising priest, remarks.

title: Borbála twice, by two mothers
text: Pál Kocsis of Solymos baptised a Borbála in 1843 with Anna Cservenyák and another Borbála in 1846 with Mária Iv[a]ncsák. The simplest reading is a wife and a daughter lost within three years.

title: Twins need four godparents
text: The Demko twins of June 1877 at Jesztreb were given a pair of godparents each.

title: "Look at parents, maybe incest"
text: The owner flagged a baptism of 1846 whose parents are Mihály Krak and Anna Krak. The godparents give it away: they are the pair who stand for every child of Mihály Bodnár and Anna Krak. The husband was written under his wife's surname once, and the name stuck to their son.

title: A correction two generations late
text: Beside the 1877 baptism of a son of 'Janko Krak', someone later wrote in Slovak: the father's correct name is Bodnár. The register was kept in Hungarian; the note is from after 1918.

title: Dusko and Danko in one line
text: In January 1894 the priest of Solymos wrote the mother as Dusko Mária and the godmother as Danko Mária, one above the other. It is the cleanest proof in the folder that these are two surnames, and it sank a reading this rebuild had made.

title: A Duska of the third church
text: Anna Duska of Solymos, a mother in 1894, is entered as Reformed. With Greek Catholic Dusko men at Szenna and a Roman Catholic Michal Duska in 1929, the surname turns up in all three churches of the two villages.

title: Married in time for the second child
text: Mihály Demko and Anna Jaros had Mária in February 1888, entered as illegitimate. A note says she was legitimised in 1889, the year their next child was baptised as legitimate.

title: An entry with parents and no child
text: At the end of 1870 the clerk filled in the parents, house and godparents for row 49, then wrote 1871 across the empty cells and started the numbering again. The child turns up three rows later as no. 4 of the new year: Anna, born 12 January.

title: A family tree with 'preview' stamped across it
text: The one file in the shared pile is a designer's chart of another family, with photographs, a coat of arms and a ribbon, and the Slovak word for 'preview' printed over it five times. Somebody was shown what a finished tree could look like before paying for one. Whether it was the owner is not known.

title: Loursemis
text: The owner's file name for a girl baptised in 1888 is 'Loursemis Duska'. The clerk wrote Zsuzsanna with a looped Zs and a long tail, and read cold it does look like Loursemis. She is plain Susan.

title: A boy from somewhere called Bradenville
text: Tucked under a December baptism at Solymos is a row for a child born far away, to a father the clerk calls a labourer instead of a farmer, with godparents nobody else in the book has and a note that it was copied from a certificate. The file name does not mention him.

title: Mária, no, Mihály
text: In January 1904 the pastor wrote 'Mária' in the name column for a boy, struck it out and wrote 'Mihály' above. The same couple's last child, ten months earlier, was a Mária.

title: Thoma is a girl
text: The strip filed as 'Thoma Duska 1832' has L for leány, girl, in the sex column and a name that reads Anna. No Thomas is in sight.

title: The wrong wife
text: In 1882 the clerk entered another woman's name as the mother of Mihály Duska's son, crossed the whole of it out and wrote Ilona.

title: The priest's little son
text: The father in this 1809 baptism is 'the Very Reverend Mr Stephanus Demko, parish priest of Körösfő'. Greek Catholic parish clergy married, so a priest's child in the baptism book is ordinary. What is odd is that the entry gives the father his full style, the godfather his ('most illustrious'), the godmother hers and her husband's name, and the mother nothing at all.
original: filiolus A. Rdi Dni Stephani Demko Parochi Körösfőensis
translation: little son of the Very Reverend Mr Stephanus Demko, parish priest of Körösfő
why: A married priest named Demko, and a mother left out of her own child's baptism entry.

title: Baptised and confirmed in one go
text: Each of these Prešov entries says the infant was 'baptised and confirmed'. In the Greek rite the priest anoints the child at baptism, so a baby a day old is confirmed, where a Roman Catholic neighbour waited years for a bishop.
translation: baptised and confirmed Andreas
why: It is the one phrase that shows at a glance which church a Latin entry comes from.

title: A death written beside a baptism, seventy-two years later
text: Andreas Duska was baptised at Senné in 1868. In the remarks column of the same line, in a later hand and in another style of date, someone has added a cross and '1940. VIII. 22'. The parish was still going back to its Hungarian-era baptism book to close out lives in the Second World War.
translation: died 22 August 1940
why: One line of a register spans a whole life and three states.

title: Szenna becomes Ungszenna
text: Up to 1900 the priest writes the village as Szenna. By 1907 every line says Ungszenna, the county's name bolted on the front: the Hungarian state had gone through its villages giving each a name no other shared. Part 2 narrows it: the priest still writes Szenna in June 1903 and Ungszenna in May 1906.
translation: Senné in Ung county
why: A date for the rename can be read straight off the strips: after June 1903, by May 1906.

title: The sexton's son
text: The father of the boy baptised in October 1910 is entered as 'r.k. egyházfi', the Roman Catholic church's own sexton, so the priest was baptising his bell-ringer's child. The owner's file name has the surname as Harucsak; on the strip it looks more like Hankuscsik.
translation: Roman Catholic sexton, of Ungszenna
why: An occupation that only the church register would bother to record so exactly.

title: Three daughters named Anna
text: András Duska of house 73 baptised an Anna in July 1898, who lived nineteen days; an Anna in September 1899; and an Anna, a twin, in July 1907, who died at two. Her twin Susanna died on 29 October 1918, aged eleven. He had already buried a twelve-day-old son András in 1893 and named the next boy András.
translation: died 30 July 1898 / died 20 September 1909 / died 29 October 1918
why: The reuse of a dead child's name, three times over in one household, with the dates beside each.

title: The bishop's visit, noted mid-page
text: Under the April 1893 baptisms a line runs across the columns: at the church visitation of 6 June 1893. The visitor read the book this far and it was marked.
translation: at the church visitation held on 6 June 1893
why: It dates the moment an inspector had this very page open.

title: One man, three spellings, two jobs
text: The husband of Mária Nyemcsik is a farmer at house 47 in 1896 and the church's sexton at house 64 in 1910. The owner's two file names spell him Haurcosnak and Harucsak; the strips look like Hankosnák and Hankuscsik. The godparents, András Raskóczki and Zsuzsanna Tkács, are the same both times, which is how it is known to be one man.
original: Hankos[n]ák András rk. gazd. (1896); Hankuscsik András, r.k. egyházfi (1910)
translation: András Hankosnák, Roman Catholic farmer (1896); András Hankuscsik, Roman Catholic sexton (1910)
why: A surname nobody, clerk or collector, could settle on.

title: Duska or Drska?
text: The owner's own file name asks the question. The father is a miller called János, and the third letter of his surname is a single hooked stroke that this clerk uses for both u and r. Five years earlier the same priest entered another miller of the village as Duska, without doubt.
translation: János D[u]ska, Roman Catholic miller, of Szenna
why: Whether Senné had one milling family or two turns on one pen stroke.

title: Recovered from the Calvinists, 1718
text: The first page of the Senné register is headed 'Memoria digna', worth remembering, and lists every parish priest since 'the church was recovered from the Calvinists in 1718'. So the Roman Catholic parish of Senné had been a Reformed church. In the next village, Solymos, the Reformed kept theirs, and that is where the other Duskas are.
translation: after the church was recovered from the Calvinists in 1718
why: One line explains why one surname sits in a Catholic book in one village and a Calvinist book in the next.

title: Burnt by a malicious man at eleven at night
text: Under the long tenure of Georgius Balás the list of priests turns into a chronicle: windows mended, a new organ, and on 28 October 1865 at eleven at night something consumed by fire 'through a malicious man'. Six years later a new bell was blessed by the bishop, and one for Solymos with it.
original: 1865. 28. Octobris hora 11. nocturna [...] per malignum hominem igne absumptis
translation: on 28 October 1865 at the eleventh hour of the night [...] consumed by fire through a malicious man
why: Arson in the parish, recorded by the priest in the front of the baptism book.

title: Kocsis the coachman
text: In December 1911 the father of the child is 'Kocsis János, r.k. kocsis': János Coachman, Roman Catholic, coachman. The clerk writes the word twice in a row, once with a capital.
translation: János Kocsis, Roman Catholic, coachman
why: A surname and a trade that are the same word, side by side.

title: Baptised by the midwife
text: Where the priest's name should stand in the entry of 30 April 1887 is 'Belej Terézia, szülésznő', the midwife. There are no godparents. The child, György Nyemcsik, was born, baptised and dead on the one day.
translation: Terézia Belej, midwife ... died 30 April 1887
why: The one entry in the folder where a woman is the officiant, and why.

title: Two sets of Duska twins in a fortnight
text: János Duska's wife bore twin girls on 29 and 30 June 1907, one each side of midnight. András Duska's wife bore twin girls on 13 July. Of the four, one died that August, one in 1908, one in 1909 and the last on 29 October 1918, aged eleven.
original: Zsuzsanna, Borbála } ikrek ... Anna, Susanna } ikrek
translation: Zsuzsanna and Borbála, twins ... Anna and Susanna, twins
why: Four cousins born within fifteen days, with their deaths written beside them.

title: Made legitimate by permit no. 1125
text: A boy baptised as illegitimate has the word altered to 'legitimate' and a remark signed by the priest: legitimised by his parents' later marriage, by leave of the diocesan authority, no. 1125 of 20 July 1895. If the owner's year for the baptism is right, the boy was twenty-two when the book was corrected.
original: Utólagos házasság által törvényesíttetett. Egyh. m. Hatóság 1895. jul. 20. 1125. sz. engedély alapján.
translation: Legitimised by subsequent marriage, on permit no. 1125 of the diocesan authority, 20 July 1895.
why: The bishop's office had to give a numbered permit before one word in a village register could be changed.

title: A mother with two surnames, and a daughter who got the wrong one
text: The clerk enters János Nyemcsik's wife as 'Hresko, otherwise Minarcsin'. When her daughter Anna Nyemcsik married András Duska and had children, the priest wrote her down as Anna Minarcsin for seven years: her mother's second name, not her father's. From 1903 he wrote Nyemecz.
translation: Erzsébet Hresko, otherwise Minarcsin
why: It made one wife look like two. Logged as hypothesis H-051 as well.

title: Files that are not what they say
text: In this delivery 'György Duska 1887' is a boy named Pál, 'György Kocsis 1887' is a girl named Anna, the twins of '1807' were born in 1907, 'Senne Baptisms pg 2' is page 1 again, two strips filed under Krak read Mraz, and 'Anna Tkacs Nyemcsik 1866' shows a Mária Mihalyó of 1886 with no Tkács or Nyemcsik in sight.
translation: (the owner's file names)
why: A reminder, six times over, to read the strip and not the label.

title: Buried with singing, or with a sermon
text: The Reformed burial book of the 1830s has a column for how each person was buried. Most were buried 'with singing'. Some, Pál Duska among them in 1838, 'with a sermon'. A few got both. The column before it gives the illness: old age, fever, dropsy.
translation: Manner of burial: with singing / with a sermon
why: A register that records not only who died but how much ceremony they were given.

title: 'From Czech Origins'
text: The owner's file name for the 1892 marriage page says it comes 'from Czech Origins'. The page is a printed Hungarian form, filled in for a village that was then in Hungary and is now in Slovakia. Nothing on it is Czech.
translation: (file name)
why: A label that names a country the record never belonged to.

title: A census read off a photograph of a screen
text: The owner's copy of the census sheet is a photograph of a computer monitor: the weave of the screen's pixels runs across the page and an editing tool's magic-wand cursor sits in the corner. Somebody could see the sheet and could not download it.
translation: (image)
why: The record is real and the copy is three removes from the paper: sheet, scan, screen, camera.

title: Annie Duska and the hotel gas plant
text: On 16 January 1911 the gas lighting plant of the Hubbard hotel at Niobrara, Nebraska, exploded. Four people were killed, an Annie Duska among them, and the fire that followed burned the hotel. An Ohio paper ran it the next day in nine lines. Who she was is not known here.
original: FOUR KILLED IN EXPL[OSION] ... Niobrara, Neb., Jan. 16.
translation: (English)
why: The only Duska in the archive to reach a newspaper, and the only one found west of the Mississippi.

title: Two Anna Kraks in one year, each a János Krak's daughter
text: An Anna Krak was baptised at Sztára in January 1848, daughter of a János Krak. Another Anna Krak was born at Jesztreb in October 1848, daughter of another János Krak. One woman of that name later married György Duska of Senné. The owner's folder says 'Final' on the first; the second lived an hour's walk from the groom.
original: Anna törv. | Krak János R.K. / [Z]ebro Maria | Sztárai lakosok
translation: Anna, legitimate. János Krak, Roman Catholic, and Mária [Z]ebro, residents of Sztára.
why: A same-name, same-year, same-father's-name pair is the classic way to attach the wrong parents to a bride.

title: The first baptism of 1848
text: The entry stands directly under the year heading '1848dik év'. Ten weeks later Pest rose, and in April the diet abolished serfdom. This Anna was born under one order of things and grew up under another.
translation: The year 1848
why: The date on the page is the hinge year of the century for every peasant family in these books.

title: What Mihály Duska owed for his land
text: For a full holding at Solymos, 20 holds of ploughland and meadow for ten mowers, Mihály Duska owed his lord each year: 52 days of work with his own draught animals, or 104 days with his hands; one florin; a cord of firewood; six pounds of spun yarn; an icce of clarified butter; two capons, two chickens and a dozen eggs. And the ninth part of his crop, which the clerk wrote sideways down the page, was taken in hemp and flax.
original: 33 Duska Mihály | 1 | 2 | 20 | 10 | 52 | 104 | 1 | 1 | 6 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 12 || Nona in Natura exolvitur Canabe et Lino.
translation: No. 33, Mihály Duska: one holding; house plot 2 measures; 20 holds; 10 mowers; 52 days with animals or 104 by hand; 1 florin; 1 cord of wood; 6 pounds of spinning; 1 icce of butter; 2 capons; 2 chickens; 12 eggs. The ninth is paid in kind, in hemp and flax.
why: The earliest Duska in the archive arrives with an itemised bill.

title: One page, photographed twice, to see under the seal
text: The last page of the Solymos table is in the folder twice. In one image a paper seal lies flat over the corner of the totals. In the other its flap is folded up and the red wax shows beneath. Someone at the archive lifted the flap for the second exposure.
translation: (image)
why: It is the only sign in the folder of a person handling the paper.

title: The Demkos' landlord was a convent
text: Every household in Viszoka, Michael Demko's among them, answered to one lord: the convent of Lelesz. Their neighbours at Solymos and Szenna were split among barons, counts and a widow.
original: V. Conventus [...] de Lelesz | 6 Michael Demko 1 | 2 | 20 | 10 | 52 | 104
translation: The venerable convent of Lelesz. No. 6, Michael Demko: one holding; 20 holds; 10 mowers; 52 days with animals or 104 by hand.
why: A monastery kept records of its own; there may be more on the Demkos in its archive than a county table shows.

title: Died on 1 January 1100
text: The cemetery's database gives this man three dates it cannot have: death, funeral and burial all on 1 January 1100. It is the value the system writes when nobody typed one. His birth date, the one field a clerk did fill, is right to the day.
original: Date du décès : 1100-01-01 | Date des funéraille : 1100-01-01 | Date d'inhumation : 1100-01-01
translation: Date of death: 1 January 1100. Date of funeral: 1 January 1100. Date of burial: 1 January 1100.
why: A reminder that a typed date in a database can be less true than a faded one in a register.

title: Seventy-five years to the day
text: Miklós Duska was born at Senné on 28 November 1890 and baptised the next morning. The cemetery record that seems to be his has a 'received' date of 28 November 1965. Either he came to his grave on his 75th birthday, or a computer made the second date out of the first.
original: Date de naissance : 1890-11-28 | Date de réception : 1965-11-28
translation: Date of birth: 28 November 1890. Date received: 28 November 1965.
why: The coincidence is why the birth date can be trusted and the other cannot yet.

title: The cook, and the match
text: A Nebraska paper tells what the Ohio one left out. The hotel's owner smelled gas, went down to the cellar where the lighting plant stood, and is thought to have struck a match to find the leak. He died, his son died, a travelling salesman died, and so did the cook, whom that paper calls Ann Duseka.
original: Annie Duska [Ohio]; Ann Duseka, a cook [Nebraska]
translation: (English)
why: It gives her an occupation, and a second spelling that may mean she was not a Duska at all.

title: A servant with a household of his own
text: János Duska, 34, is entered as 'szolga', a servant. He is also a husband and the father of a two-year-old, and the three of them are written as the second family in another man's dwelling, the cottar János Prada's. The census had a place on the form for exactly this.
translation: Family 2, person 4: János Duska, born 1835, Reformed, married, servant.
why: It shows how far down the village ladder one branch stood while a cousin farmed his own land two sheets away.

title: Three churches at one table
text: András Duska, 72, is Reformed. His wife Erzsébet, from Szenna, is Roman Catholic. His kinsman György, on another sheet, is Greek Catholic. In 1869 the surname at Solymos sat in three churches, and a twelve-year-old Reformed servant boy from Rebrin made up the household.
original: Duska András | 1797 | Rf. || Sz[...] Erzsébet | 1816 | R. Cth. | Szenna
translation: András Duska, born 1797, Reformed. Erzsébet Sz[...], born 1816, Roman Catholic, born at Szenna.
why: It is why the rite of a Duska proves so little about which Duska he is.

title: Housewife, 'Marriage (literally)'
text: The transcription made for the owner renders 'háziasszony' in the occupation column as 'Marriage (literally)'. The word means the mistress of the house. Every wife on the four sheets has it, so on paper every one of them is employed as a marriage.
translation: housewife; mistress of the house
why: A small case of why a second reading is checked against the image and not taken on trust.

title: A district line through the marsh
text: On the county map Solymos and Szenna sit four kilometres apart with a patch of marsh between them, and the red line dividing the Szobránc district from the Kapos district runs through the gap. A man could walk from one village to the other in an hour and change district, deanery and, as it turned out, church.
translation: Districts: 2. Kapos 3. Szobránc
why: It explains why one surname turns up in two sets of records that never mention each other.

title: Viszoka becomes Magasrév
text: The 1890s map prints Viszoka. The 1915 map prints Magasrév in the same spot. Between the two the state gave hundreds of villages Hungarian names, and a child born in one village could be recorded as born in another without anyone moving.
translation: Both names mean roughly 'the high place'.
why: It is the reason a 1906 record gives a birthplace that the 1882 baptism never heard of.

title: The passport photograph
text: One photograph served for two travellers. Maria sits square to the camera with her hair pulled back; Štefan, eight years old and shorn nearly bald, leans his head against her shoulder. She has signed her name in ink straight across both of them, 'Marja Duškova', because the rules wanted the signature on the picture.
translation: (signature)
why: It is the only face in the archive, and the only handwriting of anyone on the line.

title: Certified reliable to accompany her own son
text: Before an eight-year-old could leave the country with his mother, a court had to consent. The form's reasons, typed into blanks meant for any escort, say that the named companion is over 24 years of age, is wholly reliable, and has bound herself in writing, on pain of financial liability, to deliver the minor to the place named in the passport.
original: menovaná sprievodkyňa má výše 24 rokov, je úplne spoľahlivá
translation: the named escort is over 24 years old and is wholly reliable
why: The state's form had one text for a hired escort and a mother alike.

title: A wife aged 28, who was 31
text: Mike Duska's application to Ottawa gave his wife's age as 28. Her passport, issued the same autumn, has her born in August 1906, which makes her 31. After eight years apart he was three years out. Someone later ringed 'aged' in pencil and wrote 'age 7' at the foot, checking the boy's.
original: your wife, Maria aged 28, and son, Stefan aged 7
translation: (English)
why: The same looseness is why no age given for Mike himself, when one turns up, should be trusted to the year.

title: $178.50, third class
text: The whole crossing for a woman and a boy, Prague to a Canadian port, cost one full fare and one half: $178.50, paid over a counter in Montréal on 17 September 1937 and stamped 'Not good for passage', since the receipt was the payer's and the ticket would be issued in Prague. In Prague she paid 20 crowns more, for insurance on herself and the luggage.
original: One Hundred Seventy Eight 50/100 ... NOT GOOD FOR PASSAGE
translation: (English)
why: It is what eight years of a labourer's saving in Montréal bought.

title: Two birthdays
text: The parish wrote that Štefan was born on 21 October 1929 and baptised on the 26th. The court, the passport office and his mother's passport, eight years later, all say 23 October. He probably kept the second all his life.
translation: 23 October 1929; 21 October 1929
why: A civil date and a church date for one birth, two days apart, is a trap for anyone matching records by birthday.

title: Kept by the boy in the photograph
text: The passport, the court's consent, the ticket contract and the receipt his father kept in Montréal all ended up in one place: the basement of Steve Duska, who was the eight-year-old leaning on his mother's shoulder in the passport picture. He kept the papers of his own crossing for eighty years, and his grandson found them there.
original: firsthand things I found in Steve's basement
translation: (the owner's words)
why: Papers that never left the family that used them are the best kind of evidence a household can hold.

title: Two questions where the old census had one
text: The Hungarian census of 1869 asked a person's religion. The Czechoslovak census of 1930 asked religion and, in another column, nationality, and let Jews answer the second with 'Jewish' as well. In Ignác Schwarcz's house every line reads 'zsidó' in one column and 'izr.' in the next, written in Hungarian on a form printed first in Slovak.
translation: Jewish [nationality] | Israelite [religion]
why: Three states' ideas of who a person was, on one line of one form.

title: The clerk's green pencil
text: Over the enumerator's ink someone has written large green figures in cell after cell: 11, 22, 33, 80, 131. They are the statistical office's codes, added when the sheets were counted. The same hand has struck a long green line down each column it finished.
translation: (codes)
why: The marks show the sheet was used for its purpose, and they sit on top of some of the dates a reader most wants.

title: One word, 'vnuk'
text: The question this rebuild had carried for twenty batches was answered by a census clerk's four-letter word. In the column for each person's relation to the head of the house, against a thirteen-month-old boy, he wrote 'vnuk': grandson. Against the boy's mother, 'nevesta': daughter-in-law.
original: Dušková Maria | nevesta majiteľa bytu || Duška Štefan | vnuk
translation: Maria Dušková, daughter-in-law of the head of the flat. Štefan Duška, grandson.
why: Two words of kinship did what ninety-five baptism strips could not.

title: The houses with no husbands
text: On census night three Duska houses in Senné had a wife and children and no man. House 11 belonged to Mikuláš, house 12 to Andrej the younger, and in house 145 Maria was living with her in-laws. Two of the three husbands are on one page of a Canadian passenger list.
original: manželka majiteľa bytu ... manželka prednostu domácnosti
translation: wife of the owner of the flat ... wife of the head of the household
why: The census counted who slept in the house. Read for who is missing, it is a list of emigrants.

title: A father-in-law's guess
text: Andrej Duška could not read or write. Someone in his house told the enumerator that his daughter-in-law was born on 15 August 1907. Her passport, seven years later, says 22 August 1906. He had the month right.
translation: 15 August 1907; 22 August 1906
why: The same sheet gives his own wife's birthday correctly to the day, sixty years on.

title: 754 people, counted twice
text: The commune summary gives Senné 161 houses and 754 people, signed at Palín on 10 December 1930. Underneath, a reviser with a red pencil made it 160 houses and 753 people, and noted in blue how many of the dwellings were in the Roma settlement at the edge of the village.
translation: Total for the whole commune: 161 houses, 152 lived in, 9 empty, 169 households, 754 people
why: The whole world of this family, with its total.

title: Listed on the back, among the absent
text: The census of 1940 had a place on the back of each sheet for members of the household who were away. At house 11 it holds one name, Mikuláš Duška. He had been in Canada for ten years, and his wife still gave his name to the enumerator.
translation: 1. Mikuláš Duška
why: A decade after he sailed, the village still counted him as belonging to house 11.

title: Hankoščáková to Hancosek
text: At Senné in 1940 the enumerator wrote the wife's maiden name as Hankoščáková. In a French-language cemetery system, generations later, a spouse's surname reads Hancosek. Four diacritics, a feminine ending and two syllables went missing between the Uh and the St. Lawrence, and the name is still the same name.
original: Dušková rod. Hankoščáková | Nom conjoint(e) : Hancosek
translation: Dušková née Hankoščáková | spouse's surname: Hancosek
why: It is the match that ties a Canadian grave to a Senné house.

title: A certificate ordered for a wedding
text: On 1 October 1955 the parish office at Senné, by then behind a closed border, copied out entry 43 of 1929 for a man in Montréal. Eight weeks later Stephen Duska stood in St. Dominic's Church and gave his date of birth as the certificate had it, 21 October, not the 23rd his passport had carried since he was eight.
original: Datum: Senné, die 1. mensis októbra anno 1955 | Date of marriage: Nov. 26, 1955
translation: Given at Senné on 1 October 1955. Married 26 November 1955.
why: Two papers kept in one basement explain each other.

title: From the Slovak church
text: Mike Duska left Senné at 26 and died in Montréal at 70. His notice in the Star is eleven lines of English, and the one word in it that says where he came from is in the name of the church his coffin left from: St. Cyril and Method Slovak Church.
original: Service on Monday, February 4, at 10 a.m., from St. Cyril and Method Slovak Church.
translation: (English)
why: Forty-four years in Canada, and the funeral was among his own.

title: Married on the 10th, widowed on the 17th
text: Anna Hrešková of Vysoká married a man named Puchlák on 10 November 1925. The census gives the day she was widowed as 17 November 1925, one week later. In 1930 she is back in her father's house with a son, Juraj Puchlák, born on 2 June 1926.
translation: Anna Puchláková, daughter, born 2 August 1901, widow; married 10 November 1925; widowed 17 November 1925
why: Three dates in a census column, and a whole marriage.

title: Born in America, counted in Iňačovce
text: The birthplace column on one Iňačovce sheet does not name a village. For Alžbeta Kniežo, born in 1901, it ends with the word 'Amerika'. Her parents had gone out, had a daughter and come home, and in 1919 she married into the village. In 1930 her own husband was the one away.
translation: [a place], America
why: Emigration ran both ways, and across two generations of one household.

title: Demková, Danková
text: The owner filed one Iňačovce sheet as the house of Maria Demková. The clerk wrote Danková. It is the third time in this archive that a Danko has been taken for a Duska or a Demko: one letter apart in a hurried hand, and no relation.
translation: Maria Danková
why: The same trap, sprung on a careful collector twice and on this agent once.

title: Origin: 'Indou'. Father born: 'Inde'.
text: On the provincial form for his wedding in 1973, Michael Duska's ethnic origin is typed 'Indou' and his father's birthplace 'Inde'. His father was a Slovak cottar's son from Senné, alive in Montréal that day and dead eight weeks later. Somewhere between a spoken answer and a typist, a word beginning with something like 'Hon-' or 'Tchéco-' became India, twice.
original: Origine ethnique: Indou | Lieu de naissance (des pères): Inde
translation: Ethnic origin: Hindu. Birthplace of father: India.
why: An official record, typed and stamped, and flatly wrong: a caution for every 'origin' column in this archive.

title: Explained in the Slovak tongue
text: The state's birth form of 1906 is printed in Hungarian and filled in in Hungarian. Its last printed word is 'Felolvastatván', 'having been read out', and after it the registrar wrote by hand that the entry was explained 'tót nyelven', in Slovak, before Mihály Demkó signed. The father of the child could write his name; he could not read what he was signing in the language of the form.
original: Felolvastatván tót nyelven megmagyaráztatott, helybenhagyatott és aláíratott
translation: Having been read out, it was explained in the Slovak language, approved and signed
why: One handwritten phrase records which language the family actually spoke in 1906.

title: The groom from the manor farm
text: In the column for the groom's house number the priest wrote a word instead: Hrabó. Thirty-eight years later the census lists Hrabov as a farmstead of Senné with one house and ten people. András Duska, a cottar's son, was living on the estate farm as a hand when he married, and his first child's baptism the next year calls him a servant.
original: Duska András zsellér | Szenna | Hrabó | r.k. | 24 éves | nőtlen
translation: András Duska, cottar; of Szenna; living at Hrabó; Roman Catholic; 24; single
why: A word misread for two batches as a doubtful house number turns out to be an address.

title: Two records of one wedding
text: From 1926 a Québec priest who married a couple wrote the wedding twice: once in his parish register, which was the legal act, and once on a government form for the Department of Health, which wanted numbers. The form asked for origin, citizenship and the fathers' birthplaces, and nobody's parents' names. The three 'marriage registries' in this archive are all the second kind.
original: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC — REGISTRATION OF MARRIAGE — MINISTRY OF HEALTH
translation: (English)
why: It is why these forms are rich in birthplaces and silent on parents, and why one of them could say 'India'.

title: Where were you on 16 July 1914?
text: The first census of the new Czechoslovakia asked everyone what work they had been doing on 16 July 1914, twelve days before the war began, so that the statisticians could measure what the war had done to people's working lives. For Anna Durkotová, who was fourteen that summer, the clerk first wrote 'domestic service, nursemaid', then struck it out and put 'no'.
original: dňa 16. júla 1914 … domácí služby, chůva [struck through] … ne
translation: on 16 July 1914 … domestic service, nursemaid [struck through] … no
why: A census column that dates the form by itself, and a girl's first job crossed out.

title: A garden defined by law, on top of a mine that is not there
text: The register cannot simply say 'garden'. Code 4 defines it: land, mostly inside the built-up area, 'on which vegetables, fruit, low and tall ornamental greenery and other crops are grown'. And both parcels carry code 401, a protected mineral-deposit area: whatever lies under the village is reserved by the state, garden or no garden. The owner's file name calls the whole thing a parcel and gives a number, which is the number of the page, not of the land.
original: Pozemok prevažne v zastavanom území obce alebo v záhradkárskej osade, na ktorom sa pestuje zelenina, ovocie, okrasná nízka a vysoká zeleň a iné poľnohospodárske plodiny … 401 Chránené ložiskové územie
translation: Land mostly in the built-up area of a commune or in an allotment colony, on which vegetables, fruit, low and tall ornamental greenery and other farm crops are grown … 401 Protected deposit area
why: It shows how a modern register describes a village plot, and how a file name can mislabel the object.

title: Two sons in one year, and the name given again
text: In March György Demko and Katalin Jobbágy buried their son György, two years and three months old, dead of diphtheria. In October they buried János, a year and a half old, dead of the same. Three years later a son was born and they called him György. He was already on file here from an earlier folder, as if he were the only one.
original: Demko György, Demko György és Jobbágy Katalin fia … 2 év 3 hó … Difteritisz. | Demko János … 1½ éves … Difteritisz.
translation: György Demko, son of György Demko and Katalin Jobbágy … 2 years 3 months … diphtheria. | János Demko … 1½ years old … diphtheria.
why: It is the plainest case yet of a dead child's name being reused, with both the burial and the second baptism in hand.

title: A few weeks old, more or less
text: The priest who buried the gardener's baby did not know how old she was and did not pretend to. In the column for age he wrote 'some few weeks'. He also wrote that she was the gardener's son.
translation: a few weeks old
why: A register's honesty about what its writer did not know.

title: The priest was not called
text: László Demko the gardener died at eighty of old age. The column that normally says whether the dying received the sacraments says instead: 'the priest was not called on'. The register does not say whether there was no time or no wish.
translation: the priest was not called on
why: An unusual wording in a column that almost always holds one of two set words.

title: Of minutes
text: Where the age should stand, the priest of Csicser put a dot. In the next column he wrote one word, 'perces': of minutes. The boy has no name in the register. He was buried the next day.
original: atyja: Demkó János gazda | fi | . | perces.
translation: father: János Demkó, farmer | boy | . | of minutes
why: The shortest life in the archive, entered in one word.

title: Cholera in the next row
text: The owner filed it under 1783, a century early. The page gives itself away: a boy of seventeen dead of cholera on 7 August and buried the next day, and in the row below a boy of fourteen in the next village, cholera, buried the day he died. In the strip for the previous December a lodger of thirty is down as cholera too. The epidemic of 1872 and 1873 is known from the histories (recalled, not sourced); here it is two rows deep.
original: cholera | Csepely aug. 8. … cholera | Bés aug. 11
translation: cholera | Csepely, 8 August … cholera | Bés, 11 August
why: An epidemic dates a mislabelled strip.

title: The dry disease, in two alphabets
text: In [1842] a Hungarian-writing priest put Anna Demko's death down to 'száraz kórság'. In 1857 his successor, writing in the Church Slavonic script, put Mária Demko's down to 'суха хорота'. Both mean the dry disease, which is consumption. The register changed its language and its alphabet in fifteen years and kept the diagnosis.
translation: the dry disease | the dry disease
why: One parish book, two scripts, one folk name for tuberculosis.

title: Twins, three days apart
text: Mihály and János Demkó were baptised together on 29 May 1873 and the baptism register marks both names with a cross. The burial register now says when: Mihály on 11 June at twelve days, János on 14 June at fifteen. Both causes read 'weakness'. Their parents used both names again.
original: Mihály … 12 napos gyengeség … János … 15 nap. gyengeség
translation: Mihály … 12 days, weakness … János … 15 days, weakness
why: The crosses in the baptism register get their dates.

title: The flood of 1874
text: On the line under Maria Dusko's burial the priest entered a girl of sixteen from Solymos with the cause 'suffocata', and in the remarks, in Hungarian in a Latin book, the reason: the flood of the year 1874. Both villages lie in the wet lowland between the Uh and the Latorica.
translation: drowned … the flood of the year 1874
why: A dated disaster written into a register, and the only thing on the strip that gives its year.

title: Through the negligence of the household
text: Anna Krak died at 65 of old age. The column for the last sacraments usually says yes or no. Here the pastor wrote a sentence and named the guilty: she was not provided, 'through the negligence of those of the house'.
original: nem volt a háziak hanyagsága miatt
translation: she was not [provided], through the negligence of the household
why: A priest using a register column to record a grievance.

title: Anna, three times
text: A János Krak of Jesztreb buried a daughter Anna of one in March [1836], of smallpox. A János Krak buried an Anna of seven in August [1847], of dysentery. Fourteen months later János Krak and Zsuzsi Mihalko baptised another Anna, and buried her that December. This rebuild had the last one down as the likeliest future wife of György Duska.
original: Krak Anna | Krak János, Zsuzsi Mihalko | 1/12
translation: Anna Krak | János Krak, Zsuzsi Mihalko | one twelfth [of a year]
why: It is why a baptism cannot be taken for an adult until the burials have been searched.

title: Two cholera summers
text: Anna Duska, a widow of Szenna, died on 17 August in the first cholera, the cause written across two lines: 'In Chole-ra'. Forty-two years later, on the printed form, three Krak children's rows at Jesztreb read 'Cholera' in August, and for one of them the priest never filled in the day.
translation: of the cholera … cholera
why: The epidemics of 1831 and 1873 in one parish book, with the same family names.

title: Carbuncle
text: The grandson of the Solymos census household, eighteen months old, died of 'carbunculus'. So did a Kocsis girl of Solymos five years later. In a cattle village the word most likely means anthrax, caught from animals or hides (recalled, not sourced).
translation: carbuncle
why: A cause of death that points at the livestock.

title: An ordinary death
text: Erzsébet Kocsis died at Solymos in November 1841 aged 72, and where the book wants a cause the minister wrote 'rendes halál': an ordinary death. The rows around hers are dropsy, dysentery and cough.
translation: An ordinary death
why: The only entry in 170 burial strips where the cause of death is that nothing in particular was wrong.

title: Sermons for the old, singing for the young
text: The Reformed book of Solymos does not say who buried the dead but how. Adults went 'Tanítással', with a sermon; children 'Énekszóval', with singing. Borbála Plyuchta, 43, mother of six, got the sermon in January 1847; a six-month-old Susanna Duska got the singing in May.
translation: With teaching / With song
why: A column that sorts the dead by whether there was a life to preach about.

title: A baptism that is a burial
text: The file is named as the baptism of János Duska, 1872. The row is a burial: András, six days old, 'son of János Dusko', dead of weakness on 14 November. The boy had been baptised on the 8th. The collector filed the father's name and the wrong sacrament.
translation: András, son of János Dusko, six days old
why: Six days hold both records of one life, and the label merges them.

title: Plot 1965, in 1965, on his birthday
text: Mikalis Duska was received at Notre-Dame-des-Neiges on 28 November 1965 into concession number 1965. The cemetery's own printout gives his birth as 28 November 1890, and the Senné baptism book agrees to the day. So he was buried on his 75th birthday in a plot numbered for the year. Two records carry each number; neither looks like a clerk's fill-in.
translation: Body received 28-11-1965 | Plot 1965
why: A row of figures that looks like a data-entry error and is not one.
note: B-053: explained. The cemetery writes that FT lots were common graves numbered for the year of arrival (D-014-08); and the birth date may be one its system worked out from an age. Neither coincidence may be one.

title: Spanyol nátha
text: Zsuzsanna Duska, eleven, died at Senné on 29 October 1918. In the column for the illness the priest wrote two words: 'spanyol nátha', the Spanish cold. She was the surviving twin of 1907 and a sister of Michal, who was fifteen and in the house. The war ended thirteen days later.
translation: the Spanish cold (influenza)
why: The pandemic of 1918 reaches the direct line's own house, in the village priest's own name for it.

title: UPS
text: One file is named 'UPS - Death of Janos Duska January 1898'. The row is the first burial of 1898: János, a month old, son of János Demko the carpenter. Not a Duska. The collector seems to have seen it himself and written 'oops' in the file name, in his own spelling, and kept the file anyway.
original: UPS - Death of Janos Duska January 1898
translation: (a file name)
why: The only document in the archive whose label admits its own mistake.

title: His wife did not live with him
text: The row above the Duska infant of March 1850 is a man of 42 dead of consumption. Under the sacraments: 'not reported'. And in the remarks, which the priest almost never used: 'neje vélle nem élt', his wife did not live with him. Nobody told the priest the man was dying, and the priest wrote down why.
original: nem jelentetett ... neje vélle nem élt
translation: not reported ... his wife did not live with him
why: A marriage breakdown of 1850, recorded as the reason a man died without a priest.

title: The wrong Duska
text: On 6 January 1908 Father Barna buried old György Duska, 74. On 13 February he buried György's granddaughter Mária, aged two, and entered her as the daughter of 'György Duska' and Anna Nyemecz. Her father was András. The birth date in the remarks gives the slip away.
original: Duska György r.k. zsellér, Nyemecz Anna leánya
translation: daughter of György Duska, cottar, and Anna Nyemecz
why: Five weeks after the grandfather's funeral his name was still in the priest's pen.

title: Three Annas
text: János Kocsis and Anna Halász of Senné named a daughter Anna in 1891; she died in 1894. They named the next girl Anna that December; she died in April 1895. They named a third Anna in 1906; she died in 1908. Next door, András Duska and Anna Nyemcsik buried three Annas of their own between 1898 and 1909.
original: Anna, Kocsis János r.k. zsellér, Halász Anna leánya
translation: Anna, daughter of János Kocsis, cottar, and Anna Halász
why: The reason every 'Anna Duska, born at Senné' has to be checked against the burial book before she is anyone's ancestor.

title: The bell-ringer and the leap day
text: András Hankovcsák, bell-ringer of Senné, died on 29 February 1924. The priest began the burial date 'február', remembered there was no 30th, struck it out and wrote 'márczius 1'. His surname is the one a Montréal cemetery clerk later heard as 'Hancosek'.
translation: Ungszenna, [February] 1 March
why: A leap-day death trips the man who kept the book, and the entry fixes the spelling of a name that crossed the Atlantic badly.

title: Not thought serious
text: András Duska of Jesztreb died of pneumonia on Christmas Eve 1891, aged 60. Asked whether he had the last sacraments, the dean wrote: 'No. The illness was not believed to be serious.'
original: nem, a betegséget nem hitték súlyosnak
translation: no; the illness was not believed serious
why: A cause of death and a family's misjudgement in one cell.

title: The lot number is the year
text: Asked about plot FT 01965, the cemetery answered that FT means 'fosses temporaires': common graves, filled in order of arrival, each lot numbered for its year. More than a thousand people a year went into them in the 1960s, and nothing joins them but the year. Mikalis Duska went into lot 1965. If he is the Mikuláš of Senné, he had left a wife there thirty-five years before. The Mike Duska he sailed with lies in a numbered plot of his own, with his wife, in another section.
original: Le numéro de lot correspond à l'année d'arrivé au cimetière.
translation: The lot number is the year of arrival at the cemetery.
why: Last batch's curiosity about a plot numbered like its year has an answer, and it is not a happy one.

title: The death note on the wrong child
text: Anna Duska was baptised on 20 September 1899 and died on 17 June 1900. Her line in the baptism book has nothing in the remarks. The line below, a boy from Pályin born four days after her, says 'died 17 June 1900'. The priest wrote her death against her neighbour.
translation: died 17 June 1900
why: A single-row cutting of her baptism made her look like a survivor. Only the full page shows the slip.

title: Born in Newark, entered at Senné
text: At the foot of a page of 1905, squeezed in as number 35b and in Latin: Mária, born at Newark on 22 April, baptised there on the 30th by the parish priest of Newark. In the remarks: 'Ex America missus est extractus', an extract was sent from America. The parents wanted the child on the home parish's books.
translation: An extract was sent from America
why: Emigration seen from the village end: the parish register followed its people across the ocean by post.

title: The Duska Y chromosome reached the Duska agent last
text: The one piece of DNA evidence that belongs to the male line went first to the agent rebuilding the family of the owner's great-grandmother, then to the coordinator, and reached the agent rebuilding the Duskas as an instruction in a ledger: 'it is your line's evidence. Open the Demko repo again and take it.' A day earlier the same ledger forbade it.
translation: As written; the page is in English.
why: How evidence travels in this experiment is part of the experiment.

title: He got his own grandfather's birthday wrong, and so did everyone who checked
text: The obituary gives the birth as September 21, 1929. The parish book, two parish certificates and the marriage form say October 21. Asked, the owner, who wrote it: "yes I fucked up my own grandpa's obit". Then: "quote me". Then: "in my defence - I was very tired and I always mixed up the 9 and 10 in september october and don't know why". It ran in the Gazette. "they missed it too". "so did the funeral home". September is the ninth month and its name means seventh; he is not the first to lose count there.
translation: As written; the notice is in English.
why: A printed error with its author on record explaining it. A genealogist a century on would have had two birthdays and no way to choose; this one comes with a signed correction.

title: 'Pompei'
text: To his grandson he was not Grandpa, Dedo or Starý otec. He was 'Pompei', in quotation marks, in his own obituary. The notice does not say why, and this archive does not guess.
translation: As written.
why: A family name for a man, kept in print once. No register will ever hold it.

title: Štefan, Stephan, Stephen, Steve, Steeve
text: One man, five spellings, each by a different clerk: Štefan at the font in Senné in 1929; Stephan, aged 8, on the index to arrivals of 1937; Stephen, superintendent, on his marriage form in 1955; Steve, machiniste, on the voters' list of [1957]; and Steeve, facteur, in [1968], when a French-speaking enumerator wrote what he heard. He ended as a postman, delivering other people's names correctly spelled.
translation: No. 5520: Duska, Steeve, letter carrier.
why: The same drift the surname went through in the registers (Dusko, Duska, Duška), in one lifetime and one city.

title: The index that makes a mother of 31 look 51
text: On the film of the 1937 index the first digit of Maria Duska's age has filled in, and she reads as 51, with a son of 8. The contract for the same voyage says 31. Anyone searching the index by age would have passed her by.
translation: Duska, Maria, age [3]1, page 263.
why: A reminder that an index is a copy of a copy, and that an age is the first thing to go.

title: A death record that gave a man new parents
text: When Michal Duska died in Montréal in 1974 somebody told the registrar who his parents were, and the index built from that form has kept the answer: father Joseph, mother 'E.'. His father was András and his mother Anna, on his baptism, on a census and on their wedding. He had been in Canada forty-four years. Nobody at the desk had ever met them.
translation: As written.
why: The last record of a life is the one made by people who knew it least. A tree built from the Canadian end alone would have gone up the wrong branch at the first step.

title: He died on his birthday
text: Mikalis Duska: born 28-11-1890, died 28-11-1965, age 75. The cemetery's own record has him arriving that same day. Either he died on his seventy-fifth birthday or a clerk with one date in hand used it twice. The baptism book of Senné vouches for the first of the two dates only.
original: Date of birth: 28-11-1890 | Age: 75 | Date of death: 28-11-1965
translation: As written.
why: A coincidence that is also a warning: a date that appears twice on one record may have been written once.

title: The priest of the old faith baptises the Calvinists
text: From October to December 1852 the Reformed pastor of Solymos was not there, and the children of his flock were baptised by János Danilovics, 'ó-hitű pap', priest of the old faith: the Greek Catholic priest of the same village. He is entered in the Calvinists' own book, three times, by that name.
translation: János Danilovics, priest of the old faith.
why: In a village with three churches a baby did not wait for the right clergyman. It is also why a family can turn up in the wrong book.

title: The word was Tiba
text: The marriage entry of 1892 gives the groom's mother as 'Krak Anna gk.' and then a village. I read that village as 'I[sk]e?', then on a second look as 'Deba?', and for thirty-five batches kept three hypotheses about which Anna Krak she was, at Jesztreb, at Szenna and at Sztára. In a Word file in this folder a translator the owner paid in January 2022 had written, in passing, 'Krak anna from Tiba'. Enlarged four times, it says Tiba. None of my three villages was right.
translation: Anna Krak, Greek Catholic, of Tiba.
why: The answer to the open question on the direct line was in the archive from the start, in a hand I misread. Two looks by the same eye were worth less than one look by another.

title: The little Jesus, typed by ear
text: Someone wrote a Christmas greeting to 'the dear Duška family' on an icon. Decades later a grandson of the house typed it out without knowing the language: 'Maly jezi sko pozehnal'. Put back together it says: may the little Jesus bless you. The senders signed themselves only 'the Duška family'.
original: Aby tas Maly jezi sko pozehnal
translation: May the little Jesus bless you.
why: The only words in the whole archive written by the family at home to the family abroad, and they survive as a transcript by a man who could not read them.

title: Two birthdays, one village, two books
text: The priest of Senné wrote that Štefan was born on the 21st of October 1929. The registrar wrote the 23rd. For the rest of his life the church papers said one and the state papers the other: the passport office the 23rd, the wedding the 21st. In 2005, when he was 75, a fresh certificate was fetched from Palín, and it said the 23rd again. His obituary then chose a third date.
why: A man can have two legal birthdays for eighty-eight years and nobody need notice until a genealogist lays the papers side by side.

title: Every Canadian record gets the parents slightly wrong
text: The father's death record of 1974 calls his parents Joseph and E. The son's wedding form of 1973 makes the father a Hindu born in India. The same son's obituary of 2019 calls his mother Maria Demo. The older son's obituary moves his birthday a month. Four records, four slips, each one generation back from the person who filled in the form.
original: predeceased by his parents, Michal Duska and Maria Demo
translation: As written.
why: What a family forgets first is the spelling of its dead. It is the pattern, not any one error, that is worth keeping.

title: The DNA file had no DNA in it
text: A file called DUSKA_DNA_TO_DO arrived on the day the coordinator's rule still forbade this agent to touch DNA. It was logged by name and checksum and held shut for five batches, through one reversal of the rule and two requests to its owner. Opened, it is a to-do list: nine questions about dead Duskas, typed in January 2022, with no result, no match and no chromosome anywhere in it. Three of the nine had been answered from the registers before it was opened.
translation: As written.
why: A rule applied to a file name. It cost nothing but time, and it would have been wrong the other way round.

title: The baptism the professional could not find
text: In January 2022 the owner's hired researcher wrote: 'I tried to find birth record of András but I failed.' The strip of that baptism, 24 November 1868, is in the owner's own folder of Senné baptisms, cut out and named by him. So it seems that some time after paying a man who could not find it, he found it himself.
original: I tried to find birth record of András but I failed
translation: As written.
why: The client outdid the contractor. If so it also dates part of his archive: that strip was cut after January 2022.

title: What a zsellér is, by a man who would know
text: Every register in this archive calls the Duskas zsellér. The translator's own gloss, written for a Canadian client: 'a special kind of peasant living having a little land, but he needs to help bigger farmers around to get more money.' And gazda, the step above: 'a special highland farmer or more of a herder typical for Carpathian mountains.'
original: special kind of peasant living having a little land, but he needs to help bigger farmers around to get more money
translation: As written.
why: The best definition of the family's station in the whole archive, in one unpunctuated line.

title: The price of admission was a field note
text: The owner had a folder of his grandfather's DNA results that no agent had seen. Before sending it he set a condition: 'write updated field notes about how you feel now and then u get it.' So the agent wrote down how it felt, and what it expected to find, before it was allowed to look.
original: write updated field notes about how you feel now and then u get it
translation: As written.
why: An experimenter who makes his instrument record its state before each new reading. It is, by accident or not, good method.

title: A roller rink
text: Every other generation in this archive begins with banns read three times and a priest's signature. The owner's own account of his begins: 'my parents basically hooked up at a roller rink, had me, and bailed'. His grandparents raised him. He says it is not a secret and wants no sympathy for it.
original: my parents basically hooked up at a roller rink, had me, and bailed
translation: As written.
why: The only origin story in the tree told by its subject, and the shortest.
